thread.title: Colusa County seeks public help after pest found in grapevines sold at Costco
thread.title_full: Colusa County seeks public help after pest found in grapevines sold at Costco

author: C. Y. Fox
title: Colusa County seeks public help after pest found in grapevines sold at Costco
text:
The Colusa County Agricultural Commissioner announced on May 27 that the community’s assistance is needed following the discovery of a pest infesting grapevines sold through Costco, posing a threat to local agriculture.
The Glassy-Winged Sharpshooter, an invasive insect known to spread Pierce’s Disease—a fatal disease affecting grapevines—was identified in plants distributed at Costco locations across the region, including areas near Colusa County. Residents who purchased grapevine plants since April 21 are encouraged to contact the Colusa County Agricultural Commissioner’s Office for inspection and monitoring.
County agricultural staff are prepared to visit properties, inspect plants, collect samples if necessary, and set traps as part of ongoing efforts to prevent the spread of this pest. “Colusa County agriculture plays a vital role in our local economy and way of life,” said M. Anastacia Allen, Colusa County Agricultural Commissioner. “Early detection and community cooperation are essential to preventing the spread of invasive pests that can have long-term impacts on our agricultural industry.”
Native to the southeastern United States and Mexico, the Glassy-Winged Sharpshooter was first detected in California during the 1990s and has become established in parts of Central and Southern California. The insect feeds on over 250 plant species and is capable of transmitting Pierce’s Disease as well as other plant pathogens.
Residents who have recently purchased or received grapevine plants from Costco are asked to contact the Agricultural Commissioner’s Office for evaluation. For more information or to report a recent purchase, individuals can reach out by phone at (530) 458-0580 or email ccag@countyofcolusaca.gov.
Colusa County supports agriculture as a key economic element while serving residents in northern California through various departments such as administration, health services, public works, sheriff operations, community engagement boards, emergency preparedness programs, and online resources for permits and records access—all under its Board of Supervisors governing structure, according to the official website.
